explain: The frame every web page starts with. head holds information, body holds what you see.
example: The first thing you type in every new .html file.

explain: Tags that name the parts of a page. They work like div, but say what each part is for.
example: A blog: header with the logo, main with the posts, footer with the copyright.

explain: div is a plain box for grouping things, usually so CSS can style the group.
example: Wrapping each product on a shop page in a card.

explain: Headings go from h1 (biggest) to h6 (smallest). p is a paragraph.
example: An article title, section titles, and the body text.

explain: A link. href is where it goes.
example: A menu that links to your other pages.

explain: Shows an image. alt describes it for screen readers, and shows if the image fails to load.
A form: a label, a box to type in, and a button.
id names one unique element. class groups many. CSS and JavaScript use both to find elements.
example: Styling every .lead paragraph, and finding #intro from JavaScript.

explain: A bulleted list. Use ol instead of ul for a numbered list.
p is a paragraph. Browsers add space above and below it.
example: Any block of normal text on a page.

explain: strong makes text bold and important, em makes it italic and stressed.
br breaks the line without starting a new paragraph.
example: Lines of an address or a poem.

explain: hr draws a line to separate two parts of the page.
example: Between two topics in an article.

explain: blockquote shows a quote from somewhere else, indented.
example: Quoting a person in a blog post.

syntax:
Run npm start to begin.

line 1
  line 2 keeps its spaces
explain: code marks a bit of code inline. pre keeps spaces and line breaks exactly.
span wraps part of a line so CSS or JavaScript can target it. It does nothing by itself.
example: Coloring just the price in a sentence.

explain: h1 to h6 are headings, from biggest to smallest. Use one h1 per page.
example: Titles of the parts of an article.

explain: mark highlights text, small is for side notes and fine print.

syntax: <!-- This is a comment. The browser ignores it. -->
explain: A comment is a note for people reading the code. It does not show on the page.
example: Explaining a tricky part of the page.

explain: Entities write special characters: © & < > and a space that never breaks.
example:
Writing "

" on a page without it becoming a tag.

explain: ol is a numbered list. Each item is an li.
A list can go inside an li to make a nested list.
dl is a list of terms (dt) and their descriptions (dd).

syntax: Open in new tab
explain: target="_blank" opens a new tab. rel="noopener" keeps the new page from controlling yours.
mailto: opens the email app, tel: opens the phone app.
href="#id" jumps to the element with that id on the same page.
download saves the file instead of opening it.
video plays a video. controls shows play, pause and volume.
audio plays sound with play and pause controls.
figure groups an image with its caption (figcaption).
example: Photos with a caption in an article.

explain: iframe shows another web page inside your page.
example: Embedding a map or a video.

syntax:
<svg width="100" height="100">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="tomato" />
</svg>
explain: svg draws shapes with code. They stay sharp at any size.
picture lets the browser pick the best image format it supports.
table holds rows (tr). th is a heading cell, td is a normal cell.
example: A price list or a schedule.

explain: colspan makes a cell wider, rowspan makes it taller.
example: A total row at the bottom of a table.

explain: label names an input; for= must match the input's id. required means it can't be empty.

syntax:
<input type="password">
<input type="number" min="1" max="10">
<input type="date">
<input type="range" min="0" max="100">
<input type="file">
explain: The type changes what the input is: hidden text, numbers, a date picker, a slider, a file picker.

syntax:
<label><input type="checkbox" checked> Remember me</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="size" value="s"> Small</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="size" value="l"> Large</label>
explain: A checkbox is on or off. Radios with the same name let you pick only one.
select is a dropdown. Each option is one choice; selected picks the default.
textarea is a big box for many lines. A submit button sends the form.
fieldset groups related inputs; legend is the group's title.
datalist gives an input a list of suggestions while you type.
nav holds the main links. main holds the page's main content (only one per page).
example: The menu at the top of a website.

explain: section is a part of the page, article is something that stands alone, aside is extra info on the side.
example: A blog: posts are articles, the sidebar is an aside.

explain: charset lets the page show any language. viewport makes it fit phone screens.
example: The first lines of every page's head.

syntax:
<title>My page</title>
<meta name="description" content="What this page is about">
<link rel="icon" href="logo.png">
explain: title shows on the browser tab, description shows in search results, icon is the tab's little picture.
example: Making a page look good in Google and in tabs.

explain: link loads a CSS file. script loads JavaScript; defer runs it after the page is built.
example: Connecting your CSS and JS files.

explain: details hides content until you click its summary. No JavaScript needed.
dialog is a pop-up box. A form with method="dialog" closes it.
data-* stores your own info for JavaScript. hidden hides the element.
example: Remembering which item a button belongs to.

explain: lang tells screen readers the language. aria-label names a button that has no words.
example: Making a site usable with a screen reader.

explain: style puts CSS right on one element. Fine for a quick test; use a CSS file for real work.
